nameStory: The name 'cranberry' comes from early European settlers who thought the flower's curved stamen looked like the neck and beak of a crane - they called it 'crane-berry.' The 'American' part distinguishes our large, plump cranberries from the smaller European varieties that early colonists knew back home.
description: American cranberry is a low-growing, evergreen shrub that creeps along the ground in sprawling mats. Its trailing stems can stretch several feet, rarely getting more than 8 inches tall, creating dense carpets in boggy areas. The small, oval leaves stay green year-round, and in late fall, the plant produces those famous ruby-red berries we see at Thanksgiving. This tough little plant thrives in the acidic, waterlogged conditions that most other plants can't tolerate.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Deep red berries about the size of a marble, with a waxy skin that feels smooth and firm when ripe. Fresh cranberries have a distinctive 'bounce test' - they'll actually bounce when dropped due to air pockets inside.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, leathery oval leaves about half an inch long with smooth edges. They're dark green and waxy on top, paler underneath, and feel thick and sturdy between your fingers - built to survive harsh bog conditions.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats with trailing stems that root as they spread. The woody stems feel wiry and tough, hugging the ground and rarely rising more than a few inches high.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink or white flowers in early summer that nod downward on slender stalks. The four petals curve backward dramatically, exposing the prominent yellow stamens that inspired the 'crane-berry' name.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found in consistently wet, acidic conditions - bogs, pond edges, and wet meadows where the ground feels spongy underfoot and stays saturated year-round.

habitat: American cranberry thrives in acidic bogs, marshy pond edges, and wet meadows throughout New England. Look for it in areas where sphagnum moss grows and the soil stays waterlogged year-round, often alongside other bog plants like leatherleaf and pitcher plants. These specialized wetland habitats have that characteristic spongy, peaty soil that bounces slightly when you walk on it.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as bright green tips on the trailing stems. By late spring, you might spot the distinctive nodding pink flowers beginning to appear.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with small pink or white flowers dangling like tiny bells. The berries begin forming as small green orbs after pollination.
seasonality.fall: The star season - berries ripen to their famous deep red color, creating stunning crimson carpets across bog surfaces. This is when cranberry harvest traditionally occurs.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves persist under snow, and some berries may hang on through winter, providing food for wildlife. The low growth habit helps it survive beneath the snow layer.

funFact: Cranberries can survive being frozen solid in winter ice and still be perfectly edible when they thaw out in spring - Indigenous peoples knew this trick and would harvest 'ice cranberries' as a fresh vitamin source during the lean months!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with bog cranberry, which has much smaller leaves (under a quarter-inch) and tinier berries. Remember: American cranberry has 'American-sized' everything - bigger leaves, bigger berries, more robust overall. The leaves are your best bet for telling them apart when not in fruit.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with 'bearberry' - while American cranberry is sometimes called bearberry, there's a completely different plant (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi) that's more commonly known by that name. True bearberry has much larger, spoon-shaped leaves and grows in dry, sandy soils rather than wet bogs.
compareHints: American cranberry is much more robust than its cousin bog cranberry, with leaves twice the size and significantly larger berries. Unlike the upright blueberries in the same genus, cranberries have a distinctly creeping, ground-hugging growth habit and require constantly wet conditions. The trailing stems and wet habitat preference immediately separate it from all the blueberry relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its Vaccinium cousins, lingonberry is evergreen while blueberries lose their leaves in winter.
Differs from highbush blueberry mainly by size - lowbush stays under 2 feet while highbush can reach 6-12 feet tall.
Unlike lowbush blueberry which has green leaf undersides and toothed leaf edges, bog bilberry has distinctly pale leaf undersides and smooth-edged leaves.
Among its Vaccinium relatives, northern highbush blueberry is easily the tallest – lowbush blueberry stays under 2 feet, while lingonberry and the various cranberries are ground-hugging plants.
Among New England blueberries, velvetleaf blueberry is the only one with distinctly fuzzy leaves - lowbush and highbush blueberries have smooth, hairless leaves.

Among its Vaccinium relatives, bog cranberry is distinguished by its extremely small size and creeping habit - while lowbush blueberries also stay low, they form upright clumps rather than trailing mats.
Unlike highbush blueberries that grow tall and upright, early lowbush stays under 3 feet and spreads horizontally.
Among New England's blueberries, black highbush stands out for its distinctively dark berries and fuzzy stems and leaves.
Unlike lowbush and highbush blueberries which have stamens that stay tucked inside their flowers, deerberry's stamens prominently stick out like tiny antennae.
Unlike its lowland cousins like lowbush blueberry and highbush blueberry, dwarf bilberry stays extremely small and produces single berries instead of clusters.
Compared to lowbush blueberry, northern blueberry prefers cooler climates and higher elevations, with slightly rounder leaves and often more intense berry flavor.
